objective: By the end of this lesson you can list the instruments and equipment 14 CFR 91.205 requires for day VFR, night VFR and IFR, and decide, step by step under 91.213, whether an airplane may legally and safely take off with something inoperative.
why: Something is always broken on a rental or an older airplane. Knowing exactly what the rules require, and how to defer the rest properly, keeps you legal and keeps a small failure from becoming a big one.

prereading.what: Required instruments and equipment for day VFR, night VFR and IFR.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.205

prereading.what: Inoperative instruments and equipment: MEL operations, the 91.213(d) steps and special flight permits.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.213

prereading.what: Background and definitions: airworthiness, MMEL, MEL, LOA, KOEL, (M) and (O) procedures.
prereading.label: AC 91-67A, 1-2 to 1-7

prereading.what: The three ways to fly with inoperative items, operating without an MEL, and operating with one.
prereading.label: AC 91-67A, 3-1 to 5-3

prereading.what: Minimum equipment lists and operations with inoperative equipment, with the position-light example.
prereading.label: PHAK 9-9 to 9-10

warmup: During preflight you find the landing light burned out, and you plan to come back around sunset. Can you go? What would you check before you decide?

key_terms.def: Equipment that meets a 91.205 requirement in another form, such as the tapes and displays on a primary flight display.
A piston engine that can make its rated takeoff power from sea level up to a set higher altitude. Needs a manifold pressure gauge under 91.205(b).
The airplane-specific list in the POH or weight and balance papers. Items marked required (-R) are needed for FAA certification.
A list in some POHs that shows the equipment needed for VFR, IFR, day or night. Items it requires can't be deferred for that operation.
The FAA's list, by make and model, of items that may be inoperative under set conditions. The base for an operator's MEL.
An operator's approved list of items that may be inoperative for a specific aircraft. With its LOA it counts as an STC.
The FAA letter that lets a specific operator fly a specific aircraft under its MEL. Must be in the aircraft.
Putting an inoperative item in a condition that is safe for flight, such as pulling and securing its breaker. Not preventive maintenance.
A legible marker next to the item's control or indicator that tells pilots and mechanics it does not work.
Maintenance and operations steps an MEL item requires before you fly with that item inoperative.
An FAA permit to fly an airplane that does not meet airworthiness requirements but can fly safely, for example to a repair base.

body.p: 91.205 covers powered civil aircraft with a standard U.S. airworthiness certificate. You may not operate one in an operation the section lists unless it has the instruments and equipment for that kind of operation, **or FAA-approved equivalents**, and they are **in operable condition** [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]].

So "installed" is not enough. A required item that doesn't work is the same as a missing one. Each list builds on the one before: night VFR is the day VFR list plus more [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(1)]], and IFR is the day list (plus the night list at night) plus more [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(1)]].
A glass panel meets the same rules through approved equivalents. On a primary flight display, the traditional "six pack" is shown on one screen [[1:214|PHAK 8-12]].

callout.text: 91.205 is only the floor. 91.213(d)(2) also counts equipment required by type certification, the equipment list or KOEL, any other part 91 rule, and ADs [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]. Under 14 CFR, all installed instruments and equipment are required to be operative before each departure unless one of the deferral methods is used [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

check.q: Your airplane has a PFD instead of round gauges. Does 91.205 still apply?
check.a: Yes. 91.205 accepts FAA-approved equivalents, and they must be operable [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]].

body.p: For VFR flight during the day, 91.205(b) requires (single-engine land airplane items shown) [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]] [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11)-(15)]]:

head: Item
Rule wording, in short
rows: Airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic direction indicator
Tachometer; oil pressure gauge (pressure system); oil temperature gauge (air-cooled engine)
(b)(4), (5), (7). A liquid-cooled engine needs a temperature gauge instead (b)(6) [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]
Manifold pressure gauge
Only for each **altitude engine** (b)(8) [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]
Fuel gauge
Showing the quantity in **each tank** (b)(9) [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]
Landing gear position indicator
If the gear retracts (b)(10) [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]
Anticollision light system
Small airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996, under part 23 (b)(11) [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11)]]
Flotation gear and a pyrotechnic signal
Only if operated for hire over water beyond power-off gliding distance from shore (b)(12) [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]
Safety belts; shoulder harnesses
Belt for each occupant 2 or older. Harness for each front seat if made after July 18, 1978; all seats if made after December 12, 1986 (b)(13)-(14) [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(13)-(14)]]
ELT

callout.text: A TOMATO FLAMES: Airspeed, Tachometer, Oil pressure, Manifold pressure (altitude engine), Altimeter, Temperature (liquid-cooled), Oil temperature (air-cooled), Fuel gauges, Landing gear position, Anticollision lights (after 3/11/96), Magnetic direction indicator, ELT, Safety belts and harnesses. Flotation and flares only for hire over water [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]] [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11)-(15)]].

Common mistake: "the manifold pressure gauge is always required on a constant-speed prop." 91.205(b)(8) requires it only for an altitude engine, one that makes rated takeoff power from sea level up to a set higher altitude [[60:2|14 CFR 1.1]]. The equipment list or KOEL may still require it for your airplane, so check [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(ii)]].

Common mistake: "anticollision lights are only a night item." For small part 23 airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996, they are on the day VFR list too. If one fails, you may continue to a place where repairs can be made [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11)]].

check.q: Is a vertical speed indicator required for day VFR?
check.a: Not by 91.205(b); it isn't on the list [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]. Still check the equipment list, KOEL and ADs before calling it optional [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]].

body.p: For VFR at night you need everything on the day list, plus [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]]:

bullets: Approved position lights (c)(2) [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(2)]].

An approved aviation red or white anticollision light system, on **all** U.S.-registered civil aircraft. If any light of it fails, you may continue to a stop where repairs or replacement can be made (c)(3) [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(3)]].
One electric landing light, **if the aircraft is operated for hire** (c)(4) [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]].
An adequate source of electrical energy for all installed electrical and radio equipment (c)(5) [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(5)]].
One spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind required, that you can reach in flight (c)(6) [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(6)]].

body.p: Position lights: red on the left wingtip, green on the right, white on the tail [[24:223|AFH 11-6]]. Landing lights are not only for landing. They help other pilots see you, and pilots are encouraged to use them within 10 miles of an airport and below 10,000 ft, day or night [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].

callout.text: Common mistake: mixing up "night" and "sunset." Night in 14 CFR means end of evening civil twilight to beginning of morning civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]. But you must have lighted position lights from **sunset to sunrise** [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]]. So position lights must work for any flight past sunset, even before "night" begins.
If an anticollision light system is installed, it must be lit, but the PIC may turn it off when that is in the interest of safety [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(b)]].

check.q: A personal (not for hire) night VFR flight. The landing light is inoperative. Does 91.205(c) require it?
check.a: No. 91.205(c)(4) requires a landing light at night only if the aircraft is operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]]. You still need the 91.213(d) steps to defer it [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

body.p: For IFR you need the day list (and the night list at night), plus [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]:

head: Paragraph
Item
rows: Two-way radio communication and navigation equipment suitable for the route to be flown
Gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator, except airplanes with a third attitude instrument system usable through 360° of pitch and roll, installed per 121.305(j)
Slip-skid indicator
Sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure
Clock showing hours, minutes and seconds, with a sweep-second pointer or digital display
Generator or alternator of adequate capacity
Gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator (artificial horizon)
Gyroscopic direction indicator (directional gyro or equivalent)

callout.text: GRABCARD: Generator or alternator, Radios (two-way comm and nav for the route), Altimeter (sensitive), Ball (slip-skid), Clock with seconds, Attitude indicator, Rate-of-turn indicator, Directional gyro [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]].

body.p: One turn coordinator or turn-and-slip indicator covers two items: the turn needle or miniature airplane for rate of turn, and the inclinometer (ball) for slip-skid [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]. The turn coordinator shows rate and direction of turn, not bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]].

At or above FL 240, if VOR equipment is required under (d)(2), you also need approved DME or a suitable RNAV system. If it fails up there, notify ATC immediately; you may continue at and above FL 240 to the next airport of intended landing where it can be repaired [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(e)]].

callout.text: In flight under IFR in controlled airspace, report any malfunction of navigation, approach or communication equipment to ATC as soon as practical: aircraft ID, equipment affected, how much your IFR capability is impaired, and what help you want [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

check.q: Your attitude indicator is placarded inoperative. Can you file IFR?
check.a: No. A gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)]], and 91.213(d) never lets you defer an item 91.205 requires for that kind of flight [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

chunks.title: Other part 91 rules that require equipment

body.p: 91.213(d)(2)(iii) says "required by § 91.205 **or any other rule of this part** for the specific kind of flight operation" [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. Common ones:

head: Item
When required
If it is inoperative
rows: Transponder with Mode C
Class A, B and C airspace, the 30 NM Mode C veil, above 10,000 MSL (excluding at and below 2,500 AGL) and more [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)]]
Ask the ATC facility for a deviation. For an inoperative transponder the request may be made at any time; with no transponder at all, at least 1 hour before [[60:495|14 CFR 91.215(d)(2)-(3)]]
ADS-B Out
Class A airspace [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225(a)]], Class B and C airspace and other areas [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]]
Same idea: inoperative, request any time; not equipped, at least 1 hour before [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)]]
ELT
Most U.S.-registered airplanes, with exceptions such as training flights entirely within 50 NM of the departure airport [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]]
Ferry to a repair place with required crew only, or fly up to 90 days after removal for repair, with a records entry and an "ELT not installed" placard [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e), (f)(10)]]

body.p: ELT batteries must be replaced (or recharged) after more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50 percent of their useful life has expired [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]]. The ELT must be inspected within 12 calendar months of the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]].

check.q: Your transponder fails at a towered field inside Class C airspace and you want to fly to a repair shop. When may you ask ATC for a deviation?
check.a: At any time. For an inoperative transponder going to a place where repairs can be made, the request may be made at any time [[60:495|14 CFR 91.215(d)(2)]].

body.p: Most piston general aviation airplanes have no MEL. 91.213(d) lets you take off with inoperative items anyway, if every condition is met. No application or FAA approval is needed [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.1]]. It is popular because it is simple, with little paperwork [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

**(d)(1) Is the aircraft eligible?** A non-turbine-powered airplane with no MMEL, or a non-turbine-powered **small** airplane even if an MMEL exists (also rotorcraft, gliders, balloons and others) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(1)]]. Turbine-powered airplanes, and large piston airplanes with an MMEL, can't use (d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]].
**(d)(2) Is the item required?** You may not defer it if it is [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]:

bullets: (i) Part of the VFR-day type certification instruments and equipment for the aircraft.
(ii) Marked required on the aircraft's equipment list, or on the KOEL for the kind of flight you are doing.
(iii) Required by 91.205 or any other part 91 rule for that kind of flight.
(iv) Required to be operational by an airworthiness directive.

body.p: On a typical equipment list, a suffix letter shows each item's status: -R means required for FAA certification, -S standard, -O and -A optional [[22:31|W&B Handbook Figure 2-17]]. The POH carries the list for your own airplane, and it is revised when equipment is added or removed [[22:30|W&B Handbook 2-10]]. If the KOEL requires an item for a kind of operation (VFR, IFR, day, night), it can't be deferred for that operation [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]].
**(d)(3) Remove or deactivate, and placard.** Covered in the next part [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]].

**(d)(4) Make a determination.** A certificated, appropriately rated pilot, or an appropriately rated maintenance person, decides the item does not constitute a hazard to the aircraft [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]]. Done right, the aircraft is "in a properly altered condition acceptable to the Administrator" [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

callout.text: Common mistake: checking only 91.205. The PHAK's examples of failed items that must be repaired before departure include the flaps and the stall warning device [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]], and neither is on the 91.205 day VFR list [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]. Run all four (d)(2) tests every time.

check.q: A single-engine turboprop with no MEL has an inoperative cabin reading light. Can the pilot defer it under 91.213(d)?
check.a: No. Turbine-powered airplanes can't use 91.213(d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]]. It needs an MEL and LOA, a repair, or a special flight permit [[58:20|AC 91-67A 3.2]].

chunks.title: Deactivate, placard and log: who does what

head: Choice
What the rule requires
rows: (i) Remove it
Remove the item, placard the cockpit control, and record the maintenance per 43.9. Removal always involves maintenance [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(i)]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]
(ii) Deactivate it
Deactivate it and placard it "Inoperative." **If deactivation involves maintenance**, it must be done and recorded per part 43 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(ii)]]

body.p: PHAK example: position lights fail before a **daytime** flight in an airplane with no MEL. You follow 91.213(d). Deactivation may be as simple as putting a circuit breaker to OFF, or complex enough to need a certificated, rated mechanic. In all cases the item is placarded INOPERATIVE [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

AC 91-67A, the FAA's current guidance, is stricter in how it describes doing this. Turning off a switch may not remove power from the system; deactivation may mean pulling and securing the circuit breaker, or removing the equipment [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. It says deactivation is **not preventive maintenance** under part 43 appendix A, and that a person authorized under 43.7 makes the 43.9 record entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. The AC is not law, but if you choose its method you must follow it in all respects [[58:6|AC 91-67A 1.1.1]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "I'm the owner, so I can deactivate it myself as preventive maintenance." Pilot preventive maintenance under 43.3(g) covers only the appendix A(c) list, such as replacing position and landing light bulbs [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]] [[60:142|14 CFR 43 App A(c)(17)]]. AC 91-67A says deactivation is not preventive maintenance [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. When deactivation takes more than placarding a switch, get a mechanic and a logbook entry.

body.p: **Placard rules.** Legible and visible to the pilot, next to the control or indicator where practical, not covering other controls, no special form required [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]].

**Afterward.** The owner or operator must have the item repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]]. The inspector gives the owner a signed, dated list of discrepancies and placards each inoperative item left that way [[60:135|14 CFR 43.11(b)]].

callout.text: Changed: the PHAK still points to AC 91-67 (1991) and the "local FSDO" [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. AC 91-67 was canceled on November 3, 2017; the current guidance is AC 91-67A, dated 10/16/23 [[58:6|AC 91-67A 1.4]]. The rule now says "responsible Flight Standards office" [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)(2)]].

check.q: The fix for an inoperative autopilot is to disconnect a servo plug behind a panel. Can the pilot just do it and placard the switch?
check.a: No. That deactivation involves maintenance, so it must be done and recorded per part 43 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(ii)]]. Deactivation is not preventive maintenance [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

body.p: Except under 91.213(d), you may not take off with inoperative instruments or equipment installed unless [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]]:

bullets: (1) An approved MEL exists for that aircraft.
(2) The aircraft has in it a letter of authorization from the responsible Flight Standards office. The MEL and LOA together are a supplemental type certificate.
(3) The MEL is prepared within the limits of 91.213(b) and provides for flight with those items inoperative.
(4) The aircraft records available to the pilot have an entry describing the inoperative items.
(5) You follow all conditions and limitations in the MEL and the LOA.

body.p: **Never in an MEL** [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(b)]]: items required by the type certification rules and essential for safe operations under all conditions; items an AD requires to work (unless the AD says otherwise); items part 91 requires for specific operations. An MEL cannot authorize a deviation from operating rules [[58:8|AC 91-67A 1.7.2]].

head: MEL fact
Detail
rows: Where it comes from

Built from the make-and-model MMEL, or the generic Single-Engine Airplanes MMEL if the type has none. May be more restrictive than the MMEL, never less [[58:14|AC 91-67A 2.1.2]] [[58:19|AC 91-67A 3.1.2]]
Approval
LOA D095 (MMEL plus procedures document) or D195 (operator-developed MEL) [[58:21|AC 91-67A 3.3.1]]
Who may use it
Only the operator named on the LOA, the one with operational control. A dry-lease lessee can't use the lessor's LOA [[58:21|AC 91-67A 3.3.3]]
Access in flight
MEL and LOA accessible to the PIC, paper or digital. Telephone, radio or data link access is not acceptable [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1]]
(M) and (O) items
Maintenance or operations procedures that must be done before flight with the item inoperative [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.4]]
Repair interval
MMEL repair categories A to D don't apply under 91.213(a), but proviso intervals do; repair by that interval or the next required inspection, whichever first [[58:29|AC 91-67A 5.5.1]]

body.p: **Timing.** MEL relief applies to items found up until takeoff (when you start applying takeoff power). You may not take off until the deferral is complete, including any required mechanic's inspection. A failure after takeoff is handled with the AFM/POH, recorded, and repaired or deferred before the next takeoff [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.1-5.1.3]].

callout.text: Once an LOA is issued, the MEL is mandatory for that aircraft; you can't switch back to 91.213(d) [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Operators under part 91 subpart K, 121, 125 or 135 must use their MEL even when flying under part 91 [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(c)]].

body.p: **Third way: special flight permit.** Any aircraft with inoperable items may fly under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]]. It is issued for an aircraft that may not meet airworthiness requirements but can fly safely, for example to a base where repairs are made [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)(1)]]. You apply with the purpose, itinerary, crew, how the aircraft doesn't comply and any restrictions [[60:79|14 CFR 21.199(a)]].

check.q: You fly a part 135 operator's airplane on a part 91 repositioning leg. An MEL item is inoperative. Can you use 91.213(d) instead of the MEL?
check.a: No. A person authorized to use a part 135 MEL must use that MEL to comply with 91.213 [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(c)]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: go or no-go with an inoperative item

body.p: You find something inoperative before flight. Your choices are to cancel, get it fixed, or defer it [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. To decide, work through this in order:

bullets: 1. **MEL?** If the aircraft has an MEL and LOA (or its operator must use one), follow the MEL, including any (M) and (O) procedures [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a), (c)]] [[58:28|AC 91-67A 5.4]].
2. **No MEL: is the aircraft eligible for 91.213(d)?** Non-turbine small airplane: yes. Turbine: no [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(1)]] [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]].

3. **Is the item required for this flight?** Check type certification VFR-day equipment, the equipment list, the KOEL for this kind of operation, 91.205 and other part 91 rules, and ADs. Any yes: you can't defer it [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]].
4. **Remove or deactivate, and placard "Inoperative."** If removal or deactivation involves maintenance, a mechanic does it and records it per part 43 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]].
5. **Determine it is not a hazard**, and run a risk check for this flight's weather, night, airports and workload [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]] [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]].
6. **Can't defer it?** Repair it, or get a special flight permit to fly to where it can be repaired [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

head: Found before a day VFR personal flight (no MEL)
Likely result, after all four (d)(2) tests
rows: Position lights
Deferrable for day VFR (PHAK example). Not for any flight past sunset [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]] [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]]
Landing light
Not on 91.205 for day VFR, or for night unless for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]]
Tachometer, fuel gauge for a tank
Required for day VFR: no deferral [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]
Attitude or heading indicator
Not on the day VFR list; required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)-(9)]]

callout.text: At a flight review, say the steps out loud: MEL? Eligible? Required (type cert, equipment list/KOEL, 91.205 or other rule, AD)? Remove or deactivate and placard? Hazard? Write the squawk where the next pilot and the mechanic will see it [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]].

check.q: In step 3, which four things must you check besides your own memory of 91.205?
check.a: Type-certification VFR-day equipment, the equipment list or KOEL, 91.205 and any other part 91 rule, and ADs [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]].

chunks.title: Risk: legal is not the same as safe

body.p: The risk in this Task is flying with a broken item without deciding whether it is required, or without making the flight safe without it. The PIC is responsible for deciding whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight, and must discontinue the flight when unairworthy conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]].
Before flying with any inoperative item, AC 91-67A says to evaluate whether you and the airplane can safely do the planned flight in the expected conditions. Consider [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]:

bullets: Whether the failure itself could be a hazard, and whether the item is needed for this flight.
How several failures add up and affect each other.
Weather, night, the departure and destination airports, the en route environment, and diversion and alternate options.
Extra workload, fatigue and other human factors.

callout.text: Deferral is not to be taken lightly. Think about the effect of an inoperative part on the flight, especially if other items are also inoperative [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. A deferral is meant to last only until the earliest chance to repair [[58:8|AC 91-67A 1.7.4]].

body.p: **In flight.** Deferrals are not for in-flight failures; use the AFM/POH procedures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Record the failure, and fix or defer it before the next takeoff [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.3]].

check.q: Your landing light is legally deferred for a personal flight, but the trip may end at dusk at an unfamiliar, busy airport. What should your risk check consider?
check.a: Night, the destination airport, and being seen: landing lights help other pilots see you [[24:223|AFH 11-6]]. AC 91-67A lists night operations and the destination environment in its risk analysis [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]. Consider leaving earlier or choosing another airport.

bullets: Thinking "installed" is enough. 91.205 requires items to be operable [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]].
Stopping at 91.205 and skipping the equipment list, KOEL and ADs [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]].
Leaving the switch off and calling it deactivated; that may not remove power [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].
No placard, or a placard that hides other controls [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]].
Treating deactivation as preventive maintenance [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].
Using 91.213(d) on a turbine airplane, or on an aircraft that has an LOA [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].
Forgetting position lights after sunset, not just at night [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]].
Using a deferral for a failure that happens in flight [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

check.q: What is wrong with "I just leave the inoperative strobe switch off"?
check.a: Deactivation means putting the item in a safe condition, which may need the breaker pulled and secured, and it must be placarded "Inoperative" [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(ii)]].

f1.caption: Figure 2-22. Two similar flight decks equipped with the same information two different ways, analog and digital.
f1.alt: Top: an analog panel with airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter, turn coordinator, heading indicator, vertical speed indicator, manifold pressure gauge, tachometer, fuel and engine gauges, and two VOR heads and an HSI on the right. Bottom: the same airplane with a large primary flight display showing airspeed and altitude tapes, attitude, and an HSI, plus a standby airspeed indicator and switch panels.

scenario.title: A rental, a dark beacon and a trip home at dusk
scenario.setup: You rent a 1979 four-seat, non-turbocharged single-engine airplane from a flight school with no MEL for a personal trip. Preflight shows the rotating beacon (its anticollision light) is dark, and the right fuel gauge reads empty though you just watched the tank filled. You plan to leave at 1500 and return home about 30 minutes after sunset. The forecast is VFR.

questions.q: Is the dark beacon a problem for the outbound day VFR leg?
questions.a: Not under 91.205 for day VFR: (b)(11) applies only to small airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996 [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11)]]. You must still check the equipment list, KOEL and ADs, then deactivate and placard it and make the no-hazard determination [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)-(4)]].

questions.q: What about the return leg after sunset?
questions.a: After the end of evening civil twilight it is night [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]], and night VFR requires an anticollision light system on all U.S.-registered aircraft [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(3)]]. Plan to land before night, or don't fly the leg until it is fixed. Also confirm the position lights work: they must be lit from sunset [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]].

questions.q: Can you defer the right fuel gauge?
questions.a: No. Day VFR requires a fuel gauge showing the quantity in each tank [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(9)]], and 91.213(d) can't defer an item 91.205 requires [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. It must be repaired, or flown only under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

questions.q: The school's line person offers to pull the beacon breaker and tape "INOP" over the switch. Is that enough?
questions.a: The rule needs the item deactivated and placarded "Inoperative"; if deactivation involves maintenance, it must be done and recorded per part 43 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(ii)]]. Under AC 91-67A, an authorized person deactivates it and a person authorized under 43.7 makes the 43.9 entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. The placard must not hide other controls [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]]. Ask for a mechanic and a record entry.

questions.q: Everything is legal for the outbound leg. What else should you weigh before going?
questions.a: A safety risk check: the effects of more than one failure, night, the airports, the en route environment, diversion options, workload and fatigue [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]]. The PIC decides whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]].

skills.do: Given an airplane, a planned flight (day VFR, night VFR or IFR) and an inoperative item, say whether it may fly, which rule decides it, and what must be done first: MEL procedures, or the 91.213(d) tests, removal or deactivation, placard, records and a hazard determination, or a repair or special flight permit.
skills.practice: Take your airplane's POH equipment list and KOEL and walk five items through the 91.213(d)(2) tests for day VFR, night VFR and IFR [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]. Check each answer against the 91.205 lists [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205]] and the AC 91-67A steps for operating without an MEL [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1]].

quiz.q: What does 91.205(a) require of the listed instruments and equipment, besides being installed?
options: That they be in operable condition
That they be inspected every 24 months
That each be listed in the POH
That they be original factory equipment
quiz.why: The listed instruments (or FAA-approved equivalents) must be in operable condition [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]]. Approved equivalents count, so original equipment is not required.

quiz.q: For day VFR, when is a manifold pressure gauge required by 91.205?
options: Whenever the airplane has a constant-speed propeller
For each altitude engine
Only for IFR flight
Only for engines over 200 horsepower
quiz.why: 91.205(b)(8) requires it for each altitude engine [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(8)]], an engine that makes rated takeoff power from sea level up to a set altitude [[60:2|14 CFR 1.1]].

quiz.q: A small airplane was manufactured in 1982. What shoulder harnesses does 91.205(b)(14) require?
options: None, because it was built before 1986
One for every seat
One for each front seat
One for the pilot's seat only
quiz.why: Small airplanes manufactured after July 18, 1978 need a harness for each front seat; after December 12, 1986, for all seats [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(14)]].

quiz.q: Position lights must be lighted during which period?
options: From the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight
From one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise
Only during night VFR in controlled airspace
From sunset to sunrise
quiz.why: 91.209(a) requires lighted position lights from sunset to sunrise [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]]. The civil twilight period is the definition of night [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].

quiz.q: Which item is NOT required by 91.205(d) for IFR?
options: Slip-skid indicator
Vertical speed indicator
Clock with a sweep-second pointer or digital display
Generator or alternator of adequate capacity
quiz.why: The IFR list includes slip-skid, the clock with seconds and a generator or alternator, but not a vertical speed indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]].

quiz.q: Under 91.213(d)(2)(ii), which equipment list marking means you can't defer the item?
options: Marked required (-R) on the equipment list
Marked standard (-S) on the equipment list
Marked optional (-O) on the equipment list
Marked optional added equipment (-A)
quiz.why: You may not defer an item indicated as required on the aircraft's equipment list [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(ii)]]. On a typical list, -R means required for FAA certification [[22:31|W&B Handbook Figure 2-17]].

quiz.q: An airplane's owner obtained an MEL and LOA. Later a pilot finds an inoperative item. Which method must be used?
options: 91.213(d), because it is simpler
Either method, at the PIC's choice
The MEL, because it becomes mandatory once the LOA is issued
A special flight permit for every inoperative item
quiz.why: Once an LOA is issued, the MEL becomes mandatory for that aircraft [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. 91.213(d) is for operations not conducted under paragraph (a) or (c) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

options: It must be an FAA-printed form
Legible, visible to the crew, next to the control where practical, not covering other controls
It may be placed anywhere in the logbook instead of the cockpit
It must cover the inoperative instrument completely
quiz.why: No particular form is required; it must be legible and visible, next to the control or indicator where practical, and must not hide other controls [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]].

quiz.q: What does AC 91-67A say about deactivating an inoperative system?
options: It is preventive maintenance any pilot-owner may do
Turning the switch off is always enough
It needs prior FAA approval
It is not preventive maintenance, and may need the breaker pulled and secured
quiz.why: Deactivation may mean pulling and securing the breaker, because a switch may not remove power, and it is not preventive maintenance under part 43 appendix A [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. No application or approval is needed to use 91.213(d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.1]].

takeaways: 91.205 items must be installed and operable; approved equivalents like a PFD count.
Day VFR: A TOMATO FLAMES. Night adds position and anticollision lights, electrical power, fuses, and a landing light for hire. IFR adds GRABCARD.
Position lights from sunset to sunrise; night starts at the end of civil twilight.
No MEL: eligible aircraft, four "required" tests, remove or deactivate and placard, no-hazard determination.
If deactivation involves maintenance, part 43 work and records apply; deactivation is not preventive maintenance.
With an MEL and LOA, the MEL is mandatory; otherwise repair or get a special flight permit.
Legal is not the same as safe: run a risk check before flying with anything broken.
cfi_notes: PHAK 9-10 still refers to AC 91-67 and the "local FSDO." AC 91-67 was canceled in 2017; teach AC 91-67A (10/16/23) and "responsible Flight Standards office" as in 91.213(a)(2).

The rule (91.213(d)(3)(ii)) requires part 43 work and records only if deactivation involves maintenance, and the PHAK shows a pilot putting a breaker to OFF. AC 91-67A 4.2.2 is stricter: deactivation is not preventive maintenance, and an authorized person makes the 43.9 entry regardless of method. Teach the rule, then recommend the AC method; if pilots follow the AC they must follow it in all respects (AC 1.1.1).

PHAK 9-10 says the MEL, LOA, preamble and procedures document must be on board. AC 91-67A 5.1 says the MEL and LOA must be accessible to the PIC, paper or digital, and not by phone, radio or data link. Use the AC wording.

Airline and charter pilots are used to dispatch and maintenance doing the MEL work. Remind them that in a part 91 piston airplane with no MEL, the pilot runs the 91.213(d) tests, and that 91.213(c) still binds them when their company's airplane flies under part 91.

Common probe: hand the pilot a squawk (landing light, beacon, vacuum pump, one fuel gauge) and a planned flight, and have them talk through all four (d)(2) tests. Most stop at 91.205 and forget the equipment list, KOEL and ADs.
Point out the 91.205(b)(11) date: anticollision lights are a day VFR item only for small part 23 airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996, but a night item on all U.S.-registered aircraft.
Have pilots find their own airplane's equipment list and, if it has one, the KOEL in the POH before the lesson.
gaps: The sources don't contain any specific airplane's equipment list or KOEL; pilots must use the POH and records for their own airplane.
AC 91-67A Figures 4-1 and 5-1 (PIC decision sequence flowcharts) are images not readable in the source set; the step-by-step here is built from the 91.213 text and AC 91-67A Chapters 4 and 5.
No source defines "operated for hire" for the landing light rule or gives civil twilight times; pilots need other references for both.
The contents of the Single-Engine Airplanes MMEL (generic) and MMEL Policy Letters are on the FAA DRS site, not in these sources.
Experimental aircraft follow their operating limitations for inoperative items (AC 91-67A 2.4); 91.205 Category II/III and night vision goggle requirements and multiengine items are left out.

activities.title: On the day VFR list or not?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.
activities.why: Day VFR items are listed in 91.205(b) [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]. The attitude indicator and clock are IFR items [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]], and a landing light is a night item only for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]].

activities.title: Night VFR rules
activities.intro: Tap a night item, then the rule that goes with it.

pairs.r: Must be lit from sunset to sunrise
Required at night on all U.S.-registered civil aircraft
Required at night only if operated for hire
One spare set, or three of each kind, reachable in flight
Adequate for all installed electrical and radio equipment
May continue to a stop where repairs can be made

activities.title: Which rule needs this instrument?
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Attitude indicator: gyro pitch and bank, IFR
Altimeter: must be sensitive and baro-adjustable for IFR
VOR indicator: navigation suitable for the IFR route
Turn coordinator: rate of turn and slip-skid, IFR
Heading indicator: gyro direction indicator, IFR
Manifold pressure: day VFR only for an altitude engine

activities.why: IFR items are listed in 91.205(d)(2)-(9) [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]; the manifold pressure gauge is required for each altitude engine [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(8)]].

activities.title: Work out the equipment numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your airplane uses three kinds of fuses: 5-amp, 10-amp and 15-amp. You have no complete spare set aboard. For night VFR, how many spare fuses must you carry at minimum?
items.why: Three spare fuses of each kind required: 3 kinds x 3 = 9 [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(6)]].

items.q: Your ELT was removed for repair on January 5, 2027. You want to keep flying the airplane, placarded "ELT not installed," through April 10, 2027. How many days after removal is April 10?
items.why: January 5 to 31 is 26 days, plus 28 (February 2027), plus 31 (March), plus 10 = 95 days. That is more than the 90 days 91.207(f)(10) allows, so the April 10 flight is not legal without the ELT [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(10)]].

items.q: The ELT manufacturer gives its battery a useful life of 6 years. After how many years must the battery be replaced under 91.207(c)(2)?
items.why: Replace it when 50 percent of its useful life has expired: 6 x 0.5 = 3 years [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)(2)]].

items.q: Your airplane has no transponder. You want to fly through Class C airspace at 1430 local. What is the latest local time (as 4 digits, like 1200) to request an ATC deviation?
items.why: For an aircraft not equipped with a transponder, the request must be made at least one hour before the operation: 1430 - 1 hour = 1330 [[60:495|14 CFR 91.215(d)(3)]].

activities.title: True or false: deferring without an MEL
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: You must apply to the FAA before using 91.213(d).
cards.why: No application, written request or approval is required to operate under 91.213(d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.1]].

cards.s: A certificated, appropriately rated pilot may make the determination that an inoperative item is not a hazard.
cards.why: The determination may be made by an appropriately rated pilot or by an appropriately rated maintenance person [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]].

cards.s: If an item is removed, the maintenance must be recorded per 43.9.
cards.why: Removal requires the cockpit control placarded and the maintenance recorded per 43.9 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(i)]].

cards.s: An item an airworthiness directive requires to work may be deferred if it is not on the 91.205 list.
cards.why: Items required to be operational by an AD can't be deferred under 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iv)]].

cards.s: Items deferred under 91.213(d) must be repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection.
cards.why: That is the owner or operator's duty under 91.405(c) [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]].

cards.s: A large piston airplane that has an MMEL may use 91.213(d).
cards.why: Large non-turbine airplanes with an MMEL may not use 91.213(d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]]; (d)(1)(ii) covers only small airplanes when an MMEL exists [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(1)]].

activities.title: Can I legally and safely fly this?
activities.intro: You own N4127K, a non-turbocharged single-engine piston airplane with no MEL. Today is a personal day VFR flight; tomorrow you plan an IFR trip.

steps.s: Preflight: the landing light doesn't come on. You plan to land well before sunset. What do you do first?
options: Fly; a landing light isn't required in daytime
Run the 91.213(d)(2) tests: type certification, equipment list and KOEL, 91.205 and other rules, ADs
Cancel; all installed equipment must work
Call the Flight Standards office for a special flight permit
steps.why: Without an MEL you may fly with an inoperative item only after confirming it isn't required by any of the four (d)(2) tests [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]. A special flight permit is for items you can't defer [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]].

steps.s: The equipment list shows the landing light as -S (standard), the KOEL doesn't require it for day VFR, and no AD applies. Next?
options: Leave the switch off and go
Write it on the squawk sheet only
Deactivate it, for example by pulling and securing its breaker, and placard it "INOPERATIVE"; have a mechanic do and log it if maintenance is involved
Remove the bulb yourself as preventive maintenance and fly
steps.why: The item must be deactivated and placarded "Inoperative"; if deactivation involves maintenance it must be done and recorded per part 43 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(ii)]]. A switch may not remove power, and deactivation is not preventive maintenance [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].

steps.s: It is deactivated and placarded. What is the last step before takeoff?
options: Determine, as a rated pilot, that it does not constitute a hazard, and run a risk check for the flight
Get a mechanic's return-to-service signature for the whole airplane
File a flight plan noting the inoperative item
Nothing; the placard completes the deferral
steps.why: 91.213(d)(4) requires a determination by a rated pilot or mechanic that the item is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]]. AC 91-67A adds a safety risk analysis of the planned flight [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]].

steps.s: Enroute, the alternator fails. Can you defer it under 91.213(d) and continue as planned?
options: Yes, if you placard the alternator switch
Yes, because it is a day VFR flight
No; deferrals aren't for in-flight failures. Follow the POH procedure, and fix or defer it before the next takeoff
No; you must declare an emergency and land at once in every case
steps.why: Maintenance deferrals are not used for in-flight discrepancies; use the AFM/POH procedures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. The failure is recorded and must be handled before the next takeoff [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.3]].

steps.s: Back home the alternator is fixed, but the vacuum pump has failed, so the attitude and heading indicators are dead. Tomorrow's IFR trip?
options: Fly IFR with both placarded inoperative
Fly IFR if a mechanic signs a 91.213(d)(4) determination
Fly IFR using the GPS map for heading
No IFR until repaired: 91.205(d) requires both gyros, so they can't be deferred for IFR
steps.why: IFR requires a gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator and a gyroscopic direction indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)-(9)]]. Items 91.205 requires for the kind of flight can't be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

final_quiz.q: A 1975 small airplane (part 23, built long before 1996) has an inoperative rotating beacon, its only anticollision light. No MEL. For a personal day VFR flight, what applies?
options: It may fly if the 91.213(d) tests pass, it is deactivated and placarded, and found not to be a hazard
It may not fly; anticollision lights are required for all VFR flight
It may fly with no further action, since 91.205 doesn't list it for day VFR
It needs a special flight permit
final_quiz.why: The day VFR anticollision requirement covers only small airplanes certificated after March 11, 1996 [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(11)]]. It still must clear all four tests and be deactivated, placarded and judged not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)-(4)]].

final_quiz.q: Same airplane, same dark beacon. You now want to fly after the end of evening civil twilight. Legal?
options: Yes, if the position lights work
Yes, if you stay in Class G airspace
No; at night every U.S.-registered civil aircraft needs an anticollision light system
Yes, because it was certificated before 1996
final_quiz.why: Night VFR requires an approved anticollision light system on all U.S.-registered civil aircraft [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(3)]], and night begins at the end of evening civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].

final_quiz.q: Which night VFR flight requires an electric landing light under 91.205(c)?
options: Any flight with passengers
A flight in which the aircraft is operated for hire
Any flight to an airport without runway lights
Any flight by a student pilot
final_quiz.why: 91.205(c)(4) requires one electric landing light if the aircraft is operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]].

final_quiz.q: Your turn coordinator has failed. Your airplane has no third attitude system. Under 91.205(d), what does that cost you?
options: Nothing; the attitude indicator shows bank
Night VFR only
Only flight above FL 240
IFR flight, because the rate-of-turn indicator (and the slip-skid ball in it) is required
final_quiz.why: IFR requires a gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator (unless a qualifying third attitude system is installed) and a slip-skid indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(3)-(4)]]. The turn coordinator provides both [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot pulls a breaker on an inoperative system and puts the switch OFF but adds no placard. Is the 91.213(d) deferral complete?
options: Yes, pulling the breaker is enough
No; the item must also be placarded "Inoperative"
Yes, if the item is written in the logbook
No; only a mechanic may pull a breaker
final_quiz.why: Deactivation must be followed by an "Inoperative" placard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(ii)]]. In all cases the item must be placarded INOPERATIVE [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane has an MEL and LOA. During taxi you notice an MEL item has failed; its MEL entry needs a mechanic's (M) procedure. What now?
options: Take off; MEL relief covers items found after engine start
Take off and have the (M) procedure done at the destination
Return; you may not take off until the deferral, including the (M) procedure, is complete
Switch to 91.213(d) for this flight
final_quiz.why: An aircraft must not take off with inoperative items until the MEL deferral is complete; if a mechanic's inspection is required, takeoff is prohibited until it is done [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.2]]. Once an LOA is issued, the MEL is mandatory [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

final_quiz.q: You dry-lease an airplane for a month. The owner holds an MEL LOA for it. May you use the owner's MEL?
options: No; as the lessee with operational control, you need an LOA issued to you
Yes; the MEL stays with the aircraft
Yes, if the owner signs a letter
Yes, but only for VFR
final_quiz.why: LOAs go to the operator with operational control. A dry-lease lessee may use only an MEL LOA issued to them [[58:21|AC 91-67A 3.3.3]].

final_quiz.q: Which item may an MEL never allow to be inoperative?
options: A cabin reading light
A second COM radio not required for the operation
An instrument an AD requires to be operable, when the AD allows no exception
An optional autopilot
final_quiz.why: Instruments and equipment an AD requires to be operable may not be in an MEL unless the AD provides otherwise [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(b)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Your ELT ran for 35 minutes in a ground test mishap and 30 minutes after a hard landing. What does 91.207(c) require?
options: Nothing until the battery's printed date
An ELT inspection within 12 calendar months
Battery replacement only if the ELT is over 10 years old
Replace or recharge the battery, because it has been used more than 1 cumulative hour
final_quiz.why: 35 + 30 = 65 minutes, more than 1 cumulative hour, so the battery must be replaced or recharged [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Deferred items on a no-MEL airplane: when must they be repaired, replaced, removed or inspected?
options: Within 10 days
At the next required inspection
Within 90 days
Before the next flight at night
final_quiz.why: Items permitted to be inoperative by 91.213(d)(2) must be dealt with at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]].

final_quiz.q: A fuel quantity gauge for one tank fails at a remote strip with no mechanic. You want to fly to a repair shop. What is the legal path?
options: Defer it under 91.213(d) and placard it
Fly with the tanks dipped and full
Get a special flight permit to fly to where repairs can be made
Ask ATC for a deviation
final_quiz.why: A fuel gauge for each tank is required for day VFR [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(9)]], so it can't be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. A special flight permit allows flight to a base for repairs [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]] [[60:78|14 CFR 21.197(a)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Your plan: sunset is 1812 and you land at 1825, before the end of civil twilight. The position lights are inoperative. Legal?
options: No; position lights must be lit from sunset to sunrise
Yes; it isn't night until the end of civil twilight
Yes, if the anticollision lights work
Yes, if you are not carrying passengers
final_quiz.why: You may not operate an aircraft from sunset to sunrise without lighted position lights [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]], even though night begins later [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].

final_quiz.q: An airline captain flies a friend's piston single (no MEL). What makes the 91.213(d) process different from the airline MEL?
options: Nothing; the airline MEL can be used
The pilot or a mechanic must do the tests and make the no-hazard determination; no dispatch or MEL relief exists
Dispatch must approve each deferral
Only the owner can decide
final_quiz.why: An MEL may be used only by the operator it was issued to [[58:21|AC 91-67A 3.3.4]]. Under 91.213(d) a rated pilot or mechanic makes the determination [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]].
